metadata.title: Root separation for reducible integer polynomials

nodes.name: (na\"\i ve) height $H(P)$
nodes.statement: The (na\"\i ve) height $H(P)$ of an integer polynomial $P(x)$ is the maximum of the absolute values of its coefficients.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.genus: the maximum of the absolute values of its coefficients

nodes.name: Root separation $\sep(P)$ and the exponent $e(P)$
nodes.statement: For a separable integer polynomial $P(x)$ of degree $d \ge 2$ and with distinct roots $\alpha_1, \ldots , \alpha_d$, we set $$ \sep(P) = \min_{1 \le i < j \le d} \, |\alpha_i - \alpha_j| $$ and define the quantity $e(P)$ by $$ \sep(P) = H(P)^{-e(P)}. $$
nodes.statement_short: $\sep(P)$ is the minimal distance between two roots of a separable integer polynomial, and $e(P)$ its exponent relative to $H(P)$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: The exponents $e(d)$ and $e_{{\rm irr}}(d)$
nodes.statement: Following the notation introduced in \cite{BM2}, for $d \ge 2$, we set $$ e(d) := \limsup_{{\rm deg}(P) = d, H(P) \to + \infty} e(P) $$ and $$ e_{{\rm irr}} (d) := \limsup_{{\rm deg}(P) = d, H(P) \to + \infty} e(P), $$ where the latter limsup is taken over the irreducible integer polynomials $P(x)$ of degree $d$.
nodes.statement_short: $e(d)$ (resp. $e_{\rm irr}(d)$) is the limsup of $e(P)$ over all (resp. irreducible) integer polynomials of degree $d$ as $H(P)\to\infty$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: The monic exponents $e^*(d)$ and $e_{{\rm irr}}^*(d)$
nodes.statement: We further define $e^*(d)$ and $e_{{\rm irr}}^*(d)$ by restricting to monic, respectively, monic irreducible integer polynomials, of degree $d$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
differentia: restricting to monic, respectively, monic irreducible integer polynomials, of degree $d$

nodes.name: Ordering of the four separation exponents
nodes.statement: Obviously, we have $$ e(d) \ge e_{{\rm irr}}(d) \quad \mbox{and} \quad e^*(d) \ge e_{{\rm irr}}^*(d), \quad (d \ge 2). $$
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Mahler's upper bound $e(d) \le d-1$
nodes.statement: A classical result of Mahler \cite{Mah64} asserts that $e(d) \le d-1$ for every $d \ge 2$
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: The degree-two values of the separation exponents
nodes.statement: it is easy to check that $e_{{\rm irr}}(2)=e(2)=1$ and $e^*(2)=e_{{\rm irr}}^*(2) = 0$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Evertse's and Sch\"onhage's determination of $e(3)$
nodes.statement: Evertse \cite{Ev} and Sch\"onhage \cite{Sch} proved, independently, that $e_{{\rm irr}}(3)=e(3)=2$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Previously known lower bounds for $e(d)$, $e^*(d)$, $e_{{\rm irr}}(d)$, $e_{{\rm irr}}^*(d)$
nodes.statement: The following inequalities gather the lower bounds obtained by Beresnevich, Bernik, Bugeaud, Dujella, G\"otze, and Mignotte in the four papers \cite{BM1,BM2,BBG,BD}: $$ e_{{\rm irr}}(d) \geq \frac{d}{2} +\frac{d-2}{4(d-1)}, \quad \mbox{for $d\geq 4$}, $$ $$ e (d) \geq \frac{d+1}{2}, \quad \mbox{for odd $d\geq 5$}, $$ $$ e^*(3)=e_{{\rm irr}}^*(3) \geq \frac{3}{2}, \quad e^* (5) \ge 2, \quad e_{{\rm irr}}^*(5) \ge \frac{7}{4}, $$ $$ e^*(d)\geq \frac{d}{2}, \quad e_{{\rm irr}}^*(d) \geq \frac{d-1}{2}, \quad \mbox{for even $d\geq 4$}, $$ and $$ e^*(d)\geq \frac{d-1}{2}, \quad e_{{\rm irr}}^*(d)\geq \frac{d}{2} +\frac{d-2}{4(d-1)} - 1, \quad \mbox{for odd $d\geq 7$}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Collected lower bounds of order $d/2$ for the four separation exponents, from four earlier papers.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.origin_citation: Bugeaud & Mignotte 2004, 2010; Beresnevich, Bernik & Götze 2010; Bugeaud & Dujella 2011

nodes.name: Pointers to related constructions and the Remak height
nodes.statement: See also \cite{DP} for a constructive proof that $e^*(4)\geq 2$ and \cite{Dub} for the study of analogous quantities defined in terms of the Remak height (instead of the na\"\i ve height).
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Aim of the paper
nodes.statement: The aim of the present paper is to improve all known lower bounds for $e(d)$, $e^*(d)$ and $e_{{\rm irr}}^* (d)$ for $d$ sufficiently large.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Theorem 1 (lower bound $e(d) \geq (2d-1)/3$)
nodes.statement: For any integer $d\geq 4$, we have $$ e(d) \geq \frac{2d-1}{3}. $$
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Theorem 2 (lower bounds for $e^*(d)$)
nodes.statement: For any even positive integer $d\geq 6$, we have $$ e^*(d) \geq \frac{2d-3}{3}. $$ For any odd positive integer $d\geq 7$, we have $$ e^*(d) \geq \frac{2d-5}{3}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Monic reducible constructions give $e^*(d)\ge(2d-3)/3$ for even $d\ge6$ and $e^*(d)\ge(2d-5)/3$ for odd $d\ge7$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Order $2d/3$ beats the previous order $d/2$
nodes.statement: Roughly speaking, all the previously known lower bounds were of order $d/2$. There are many other questions on integer polynomials of degree $d$, or on algebraic numbers of degree $d$, for which the answer is known to lie somewhere between $d/2$ and $d$. The most celebrated one is the problem of Wirsing on the approximation to transcendental real numbers by algebraic numbers of degree at most $d$; see Chapter 3 of \cite{BuLiv}. We stress that the lower bounds in Theorems \ref{tm1} and \ref{tm2} are of the order $2d/3$. As far as we are aware, this is the first time where an estimate of order $\theta d$ with $\theta > 1/2$ is obtained for such kind of questions.
nodes.statement_short: Unlike earlier order-$d/2$ bounds, Theorems 1 and 2 reach order $2d/3$, apparently the first $\theta d$ estimate with $\theta>1/2$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Relation to Mahler's and Koksma's classifications
nodes.statement: As pointed out in \cite{Bu1}, irreducible polynomials with close roots are useful to investigate the difference between Mahler's and Koksma's classifications of real numbers. However, it does not seem to us that Theorem \ref{tm1} could be applied to this question to improve Corollary 1 of \cite{BD}.
nodes.statement_short: Close-root irreducible polynomials bear on Mahler vs Koksma classifications, but Theorem 1 does not seem to improve Corollary 1 of [BD].
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Overview of the construction and Bombieri's Thue--Siegel principle
nodes.statement: To prove Theorems 1 and 2 we construct parametric families of integer polynomials. For an integer $d \ge 4$, the reducible polynomials arising in the proof of Theorem 1 are products of a linear polynomial $L_n (x) = (n^2 + 3n +1)x - (n+2)$ with an irreducible polynomial $p_{d-1, n} (x)$ of degree $d-1$ and height of order $n$. We then show that $p_{d-1, n} (x)$ has a root $y_{d,n}$ very close to the root $x_n = (n+2)/(n^2 + 3n + 1)$ of $L_n(x)$. Say differently, we construct a parametric family $(y_{d,n})_{n \ge 1}$ of algebraic numbers of degree $d-1$ which are very well approximated by a rational number with large height (in comparison to the height of $y_{d,n}$). This means that it is then possible to apply Bombieri's version of the Thue--Siegel principle \cite[Theorem 4]{Bom} to the anchor pair $(y_{d,n}, x_n)$ to derive a rather good effective irrationality measure for $y_{d,n}$ when $n$ is sufficiently large in comparison to $d$. In his paper, Bombieri used the polynomials $x^d - n x + 1$, which have a root very close to the rational number $1/n$.
nodes.statement_short: The proofs multiply a linear $L_n(x)$ by an irreducible $p_{d-1,n}(x)$ having a root near $x_n$, yielding well-approximated algebraic numbers usable in Bombieri's Thue--Siegel principle.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Theorem 3 (lower bound $e_{{\rm irr}}^*(d) \geq d/2 - 1/4$)
nodes.statement: For any positive integer $d\geq 4$, we have $$ e_{{\rm irr}}^* (d) \geq \frac{d}{2}-\frac{1}{4}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Irreducible monic polynomials of degree $d\ge4$ give $e_{\rm irr}^*(d)\ge d/2-1/4$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Convention on the implied constants
nodes.statement: Throughout the next sections, the constants implied by the symbols $O$, $\ll$ and $\gg$ can be explicitly computed, are independent of the parameter $n$, and depend at most on the degree $d$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: The sequence $p_{d,n}(x)$ and the polynomials $P_{d,n}(x)$
nodes.statement: We want to construct a one-parametric sequence of integer polynomials $p_{d,n}(x)$ of degree $d$ having a root very close to the rational number $x_n=(n+2)/(n^2+3n+1)$. Then the polynomials $$ P_{d,n}(x)=((n^2+3n+1)x-(n+2)) p_{d-1,n}(x) $$ will have two roots very close to each other. We define the sequence $p_{d,n}(x)$ recursively by $$ \eqalign{ & p_{0,n} (x) = -1, \quad p_{1,n} (x) = (n+1)x-1, \cr & p_{d,n} (x) = (1+x) p_{d-1,n}(x) +x^2 p_{d-2,n} (x). \cr} \eqno (1) $$
nodes.statement_short: Defines $x_n=(n+2)/(n^2+3n+1)$, the product $P_{d,n}=((n^2+3n+1)x-(n+2))p_{d-1,n}$, and the recursion (1) for $p_{d,n}$.
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1

nodes.name: Value of $p_{d,n}$ at $x_n$ (equation (2))
nodes.statement: We claim that $$ p_{d,n}\left(\frac{n+2}{n^2+3n+1}\right) = \frac{(-1)^{d-1}}{(n^2+3n+1)^d}. \eqno (2) $$
nodes.statement_short: $p_{d,n}$ evaluated at $x_n$ equals $(-1)^{d-1}(n^2+3n+1)^{-d}$, hence is tiny.
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1

nodes.name: Proof of the evaluation formula (2)
nodes.statement: Indeed, (2) is clearly true for $d=0$ and $d=1$. Assume now that $d \ge 1$ is an integer for which (2) holds for $p_{d-1,n} (x)$ and $p_{d,n} (x)$. Then we deduce from the recursion (1) that $$ \eqalign{ p_{d,n}\left(\frac{n+2}{n^2+3n+1}\right) & = \frac{(-1)^{d-2}}{(n^2+3n+1)^{d-1}} \cdot \frac{n^2+ 4n+3}{n^2+3n+1} \cr & \, \, \, \, \, \, \, \, + \frac{(-1)^{d-3}}{(n^2+3n+1)^{d-2}} \cdot \frac{n^2+ 4n+4}{(n^2+3n+1)^2} \cr & = \frac{(-1)^{d-1}}{(n^2+3n+1)^d}, \cr} $$ as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: By induction on $d$: check $d=0,1$, then substitute the recursion (1) and simplify.
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1

nodes.name: Base cases $d=0,1$
nodes.statement: Indeed, (2) is clearly true for $d=0$ and $d=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Verify (2) for the two initial values of $d$.
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1

nodes.name: Inductive step via the recursion (1)
nodes.statement: Assume now that $d \ge 1$ is an integer for which (2) holds for $p_{d-1,n} (x)$ and $p_{d,n} (x)$. Then we deduce from the recursion (1) that $$ \eqalign{ p_{d,n}\left(\frac{n+2}{n^2+3n+1}\right) & = \frac{(-1)^{d-2}}{(n^2+3n+1)^{d-1}} \cdot \frac{n^2+ 4n+3}{n^2+3n+1} \cr & \, \, \, \, \, \, \, \, + \frac{(-1)^{d-3}}{(n^2+3n+1)^{d-2}} \cdot \frac{n^2+ 4n+4}{(n^2+3n+1)^2} \cr & = \frac{(-1)^{d-1}}{(n^2+3n+1)^d}, \cr} $$ as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: Assume (2) for $p_{d-1,n}$ and $p_{d,n}$, expand with (1), and simplify to the claimed value.
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1

nodes.name: Existence of a root of $p_{d,n}$ between $x_n$ and $z_{d,n}$
nodes.statement: We now show that for sufficiently large $n$ the polynomial $p_{d,n} (x)$ has a root between $x_n$ and $$ z_{d,n}=x_n + \frac{(-1)^{d}}{n(n^2+3n+1)^d}. $$
nodes.statement_short: For large $n$, $p_{d,n}$ has a root in the interval between $x_n$ and $z_{d,n}=x_n+(-1)^d/(n(n^2+3n+1)^d)$.
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1
conclusions: the polynomial $p_{d,n} (x)$ has a root between $x_n$ and

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: Observe that $$ (-1)^{d-1} p_{d,n}(x_n) = \frac{1}{(n^2+3n+1)^d} > 0. $$ By Rolle's theorem, there exists $z'_{d,n}$ between $x_n$ and $z_{d,n}$ such that $$ p_{d,n}(z_{d,n})=p_{d,n}(x_n)+(z_{d,n}-x_n)p'_{d,n}(z'_{d,n}). $$ It follows easily by induction that $$ p_{d,n}(x)=-1+(n-d+2)x+((d-1)n-(d-1)(d-2)/2)x^2+\cdots $$ Since $x_n=1/n+O(1/n^2)$, we have $p'_{d,n}(z'_{d,n}) = n + d + O(1/n)$. Thus, for sufficiently large $n$, we get $p'_{d,n}(z'_{d,n}) > n$. This implies that $$ (-1)^{d-1}p_{d,n}(z_{d,n}) = \frac{1}{(n^2+3n+1)^d} - \frac{1}{n(n^2+3n+1)^d}p'_{d,n}(z'_{d,n}) < 0. $$ Therefore, the polynomial $P_{d,n}(x)=((n^2+3n+1)x-(n+2)) p_{d-1,n}(x)$ has two close roots: $x_n$ and $y_{d,n}$, which is between $x_n$ and $z_{d-1,n}$. This yields $$ {\rm sep}(P_{d,n}) \leq |x_n - y_{d,n} | \leq \frac{1}{n(n^2+3n+1)^{d-1}} \leq \frac{1}{n^{2d-1}}, \eqno (3) $$ when $n$ is large enough. Since the height of $P_{d,n} (x)$ is bounded from above by $n^3$ times a number depending only on $d$, this gives $$ e(d)\geq \frac{2d-1}{3}, $$ by letting $n$ tend to infinity. The proof of Theorem \ref{tm1} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Sign change between $x_n$ and $z_{d,n}$ via Rolle's theorem localises a root of $p_{d,n}$; the product $P_{d,n}$ then has two roots within $n^{-(2d-1)}$ while $H(P_{d,n})\ll n^3$.
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1

nodes.name: Sign of $p_{d,n}$ at $x_n$
nodes.statement_short: Record that $(-1)^{d-1}p_{d,n}(x_n)$ is positive.
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1

nodes.name: Mean value expansion by Rolle's theorem
nodes.statement: By Rolle's theorem, there exists $z'_{d,n}$ between $x_n$ and $z_{d,n}$ such that $$ p_{d,n}(z_{d,n})=p_{d,n}(x_n)+(z_{d,n}-x_n)p'_{d,n}(z'_{d,n}). $$
nodes.statement_short: Apply Rolle's theorem to write $p_{d,n}(z_{d,n})$ as $p_{d,n}(x_n)$ plus a derivative term.
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1

nodes.name: Low-order expansion of $p_{d,n}(x)$
nodes.statement: It follows easily by induction that $$ p_{d,n}(x)=-1+(n-d+2)x+((d-1)n-(d-1)(d-2)/2)x^2+\cdots $$
nodes.statement_short: Obtain the first coefficients of $p_{d,n}$ by induction.
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1

nodes.name: Lower bound for the derivative
nodes.statement: Since $x_n=1/n+O(1/n^2)$, we have $p'_{d,n}(z'_{d,n}) = n + d + O(1/n)$. Thus, for sufficiently large $n$, we get $p'_{d,n}(z'_{d,n}) > n$.
nodes.statement_short: Estimate $p'_{d,n}(z'_{d,n})=n+d+O(1/n)$, hence $>n$ for large $n$.
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1

nodes.name: Opposite sign at $z_{d,n}$
nodes.statement_short: Deduce that $(-1)^{d-1}p_{d,n}(z_{d,n})<0$, so a root lies in between.
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1

nodes.name: Separation bound for $P_{d,n}$
nodes.statement: Therefore, the polynomial $P_{d,n}(x)=((n^2+3n+1)x-(n+2)) p_{d-1,n}(x)$ has two close roots: $x_n$ and $y_{d,n}$, which is between $x_n$ and $z_{d-1,n}$. This yields $$ {\rm sep}(P_{d,n}) \leq |x_n - y_{d,n} | \leq \frac{1}{n(n^2+3n+1)^{d-1}} \leq \frac{1}{n^{2d-1}}, \eqno (3) $$ when $n$ is large enough.
nodes.statement_short: The two close roots $x_n,y_{d,n}$ of $P_{d,n}$ give $\sep(P_{d,n})\le n^{-(2d-1)}$, which is (3).
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1

nodes.name: Conclusion via the height bound
nodes.statement: Since the height of $P_{d,n} (x)$ is bounded from above by $n^3$ times a number depending only on $d$, this gives $$ e(d)\geq \frac{2d-1}{3}, $$ by letting $n$ tend to infinity. The proof of Theorem \ref{tm1} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Combine $H(P_{d,n})\ll n^3$ with (3) and let $n\to\infty$ to get $e(d)\ge(2d-1)/3$.
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1

nodes.name: Separation bound (3) for $P_{d,n}$
nodes.statement: $$ {\rm sep}(P_{d,n}) \leq |x_n - y_{d,n} | \leq \frac{1}{n(n^2+3n+1)^{d-1}} \leq \frac{1}{n^{2d-1}}, \eqno (3) $$
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1

nodes.name: Gelfond's inequality
nodes.statement: By Gelfond's inequality (see e.g. \cite[Lemma A.3]{BuLiv}), the height of $y_{d,n}$ is $\ll n$.
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1

nodes.name: Liouville's inequality
nodes.statement: Liouville's inequality (see e.g. \cite[Theorem A.1]{BuLiv}) then implies that $$ |x_n - y_{d,n}| \gg n^{-2 \delta-1}, $$ where $\delta$ denotes the degree of $y_{d,n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Liouville's inequality bounds $|x_n-y_{d,n}|$ from below by $n^{-2\delta-1}$, $\delta$ the degree of $y_{d,n}$.
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1

nodes.name: Irreducibility of $p_{d-1,n}(x)$
nodes.statement: Combined with (3), this gives $\delta = d-1$ and establishes that the polynomial $p_{d-1,n} (x)$ must be irreducible.
nodes.statement_short: Comparing (3) with Liouville's inequality forces $\deg y_{d,n}=d-1$, so $p_{d-1,n}$ is irreducible.
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1

nodes.name: Sharpness of Liouville's inequality in $n$
nodes.statement: Also, (3) shows that Liouville's inequality $$ |x_n - y_{d,n}| \gg n^{-2d+1} $$ is sharp in terms of $n$.
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1

nodes.name: The monic quadratic $K_n(x)$ and the polynomials $Q_{d,n}(x)$
nodes.statement: In order to get a family of monic polynomials with similar separation properties as the family $P_{d,n}(x)$, we replace the linear non-monic polynomial $L_n(x)=(n^2+3n+1)x-(n+2)$ by the monic quadratic polynomial $$ K_n(x)=x^2 - (n^2+3n+1)x+(n+2). $$ Thus, we want to construct a one-parametric sequence of integer polynomials $q_{d,n}(x)$ of degree $d$ having a root very close to the root $y_n=1/n+O(1/n^2)$ of $K_n(x)$. Then the polynomials $$ Q_{d,n}(x)=(x^2 - (n^2+3n+1)x+(n+2)) q_{d-2,n}(x) $$ will have two roots very close to each other.
nodes.statement_short: Replaces $L_n$ by the monic $K_n(x)=x^2-(n^2+3n+1)x+(n+2)$ with root $y_n$, and sets $Q_{d,n}=K_n\,q_{d-2,n}$.
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2

nodes.name: The sequence $q_{d,n}(x)$
nodes.statement: For $d \ge 0$ even, we define the sequence $q_{d,n}(x)$ recursively by $$ \eqalign{ & q_{0,n} (x) = 1, \quad q_{2,n} (x) = x^2-(n+1)x+1, \cr & q_{d,n} (x) = (2x^2 + x + 1) q_{d-2,n} (x) - x^4 q_{d-4,n} (x). \cr} \eqno (4) $$
nodes.statement_short: Recursive monic family $q_{d,n}$ for even $d$, with $q_{0,n}=1$, $q_{2,n}=x^2-(n+1)x+1$.
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2

nodes.name: Divisibility of $q_{d,n}-q_{d-2,n}q_{2,n}$ by $K_n$
nodes.statement: We claim that $q_{d,n} (x)- q_{d-2,n} (x) q_{2,n} (x)$ is divisible by $K_n (x)$.
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2
conclusions: q_{d,n} (x)- q_{d-2,n} (x) q_{2,n} (x)$ is divisible by $K_n (x)

nodes.name: Proof of the divisibility claim
nodes.statement: This is easy to check for $d=2$ and $d=4$, and then the claim follows by induction using the recursion (4).
nodes.statement_short: By induction on even $d$, with $d=2,4$ checked directly and the step supplied by the recursion (4).
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2

nodes.name: Base cases $d=2,4$
nodes.statement: This is easy to check for $d=2$ and $d=4$,
nodes.statement_short: Direct check for $d=2,4$.
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2

nodes.name: Inductive step via the recursion (4)
nodes.statement: and then the claim follows by induction using the recursion (4).
nodes.statement_short: Propagate the divisibility using the four-term recursion (4).
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2

nodes.name: Multiplicativity of $q_{d,n}$ at $y_n$
nodes.statement: This yields that $$ q_{d,n}(y_n) = q_{d-2,n}(y_n)q_{2,n}(y_n) = (q_{2,n}(y_n))^{d/2}, $$ for $d \ge 2$ even.
nodes.statement_short: At the root $y_n$ of $K_n$, $q_{d,n}(y_n)=(q_{2,n}(y_n))^{d/2}$.
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2

nodes.name: Asymptotic value of $q_{d,n}(y_n)$
nodes.statement_short: Using the expansion of $y_n$, $q_{2,n}(y_n)=n^{-4}+O(n^{-5})$ hence $q_{d,n}(y_n)=n^{-2d}+O(n^{-2d-1})$.
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2

nodes.name: Existence of a root of $q_{d,n}$ between $y_n$ and $w_{d,n}$
nodes.statement: We now show that for sufficiently large $n$ the polynomial $q_{d,n} (x)$ has a root between $y_n$ and $w_{d,n}=y_n + \frac{2}{n^{2d+1}}$.
nodes.statement_short: For large $n$, $q_{d,n}$ has a root between $y_n$ and $w_{d,n}=y_n+2n^{-(2d+1)}$.
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2
conclusions: the polynomial $q_{d,n} (x)$ has a root between $y_n$ and $w_{d,n}=y_n + \frac{2}{n^{2d+1}}$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: We have $$ q_{d,n}(y_n) = 1/n^{2d} + O(1/n^{2d+1}) > 0. $$ By Rolle's theorem, there exists $w'_{d,n}$ between $y_n$ and $w_{d,n}$ such that $$ q_{d,n}(w_{d,n})=q_{d,n}(y_n)+(w_{d,n}-y_n)q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n}). $$ It follows easily by induction that $$ q_{d,n}(x)=1+(-n+d/2-2)x+((-d/2+1)n+(d^2-2d+8)/8)x^2+\cdots $$ Since $y_n=1/n+O(1/n^2)$, we have $q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n}) = -n - d/2 + O(1/n)$. Thus, for sufficiently large $n$, we get $q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n}) < -n$. This implies $$ q_{d,n}(w_{d,n}) = 1/n^{2d} + O(1/n^{2d+1}) + \frac{2}{n^{2d+1}}q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n}) < 0. $$ Thus, the polynomial $Q_{d,n}(x)=(x^2 - (n^2+3n+1)x+(n+2)) q_{d-2,n}(x)$ has two close roots: $y_n$ and $v_{d,n}$, which is between $y_n$ and $w_{d-2,n}$. This yields $$ {\rm sep}(Q_{d,n}) \leq \frac{2}{n^{2d-3}}, $$ when $n$ is large enough. Since $H(Q_{d,n})=O(n^3)$, this gives $$ e^*(d)\geq \frac{2d-3}{3}, $$ by letting $n$ tend to infinity. Let now $d$ be odd. Then we define $$ Q_{d,n}(x)=x(x^2 - (n^2+3n+1)x+(n+2)) q_{d-3,n}(x). $$ This polynomial has two close roots: $y_n$ and a root lying between $y_n$ and $w_{d-3,n}$. Thus we get $$ {\rm sep}(Q_{d,n}) \leq \frac{2}{n^{2d-5}}, $$ for $n$ large enough, and $$ e^*(d)\geq \frac{2d-5}{3}. $$ The proof of Theorem \ref{tm2} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Same sign-change-plus-Rolle argument as Theorem 1, applied to the monic $Q_{d,n}$, then a separate odd-degree case obtained by multiplying by $x$.

nodes.name: Positivity of $q_{d,n}(y_n)$
nodes.statement_short: Record that $q_{d,n}(y_n)$ is positive.
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2

nodes.name: Mean value expansion by Rolle's theorem
nodes.statement: By Rolle's theorem, there exists $w'_{d,n}$ between $y_n$ and $w_{d,n}$ such that $$ q_{d,n}(w_{d,n})=q_{d,n}(y_n)+(w_{d,n}-y_n)q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n}). $$
nodes.statement_short: Apply Rolle's theorem to expand $q_{d,n}(w_{d,n})$ around $y_n$.
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2

nodes.name: Low-order expansion of $q_{d,n}(x)$
nodes.statement: It follows easily by induction that $$ q_{d,n}(x)=1+(-n+d/2-2)x+((-d/2+1)n+(d^2-2d+8)/8)x^2+\cdots $$
nodes.statement_short: Obtain the first coefficients of $q_{d,n}$ by induction.
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2

nodes.name: Upper bound for the derivative
nodes.statement: Since $y_n=1/n+O(1/n^2)$, we have $q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n}) = -n - d/2 + O(1/n)$. Thus, for sufficiently large $n$, we get $q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n}) < -n$.
nodes.statement_short: Estimate $q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n})=-n-d/2+O(1/n)$, hence $<-n$ for large $n$.
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2

nodes.name: Opposite sign at $w_{d,n}$
nodes.statement_short: Deduce $q_{d,n}(w_{d,n})<0$, so a root lies between $y_n$ and $w_{d,n}$.
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2

nodes.name: Even degree: separation and height of $Q_{d,n}$
nodes.statement: Thus, the polynomial $Q_{d,n}(x)=(x^2 - (n^2+3n+1)x+(n+2)) q_{d-2,n}(x)$ has two close roots: $y_n$ and $v_{d,n}$, which is between $y_n$ and $w_{d-2,n}$. This yields $$ {\rm sep}(Q_{d,n}) \leq \frac{2}{n^{2d-3}}, $$ when $n$ is large enough. Since $H(Q_{d,n})=O(n^3)$, this gives $$ e^*(d)\geq \frac{2d-3}{3}, $$ by letting $n$ tend to infinity.
nodes.statement_short: For even $d$, $\sep(Q_{d,n})\le 2n^{-(2d-3)}$ and $H(Q_{d,n})=O(n^3)$ give $e^*(d)\ge(2d-3)/3$.
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2

nodes.name: Odd degree case
nodes.statement: Let now $d$ be odd. Then we define $$ Q_{d,n}(x)=x(x^2 - (n^2+3n+1)x+(n+2)) q_{d-3,n}(x). $$ This polynomial has two close roots: $y_n$ and a root lying between $y_n$ and $w_{d-3,n}$. Thus we get $$ {\rm sep}(Q_{d,n}) \leq \frac{2}{n^{2d-5}}, $$ for $n$ large enough, and $$ e^*(d)\geq \frac{2d-5}{3}. $$ The proof of Theorem \ref{tm2} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: For odd $d$, multiply by $x$ to get $\sep(Q_{d,n})\le 2n^{-(2d-5)}$ and $e^*(d)\ge(2d-5)/3$.

nodes.name: Fibonacci numbers $F_k$
nodes.statement: Let $F_k$ denote the $k$th Fibonacci number defined by the recursion $F_0=0$, $F_1=1$ and $F_k=F_{k-1}+F_{k-2}$ for $k \ge 2$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: Fibonacci numbers in the expansion of $x_n$
nodes.statement: Note that Fibonacci numbers appear in the asymptotic expansion of $x_n = (n+2) / (n^2 + 3n + 1)$, namely $$ x_n = 1/n-1/n^2+2/n^3-5/n^4+13/n^5-34/n^6+ \cdots - (-1)^k F_{2k-3}/n^{k} + \cdots $$
nodes.statement_short: The asymptotic expansion of $x_n$ has Fibonacci numbers as coefficients.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: The polynomials $s_{d,n}(x)$ and $r_{d,n}(x)$
nodes.statement: For $d\geq 0$, we first define monic polynomials $s_{d,n}(x)$ with a root close to $x_n $ by $$ s_{d,n} (x)=(-1)^{d-1}(F_{d-1}p_{d,n}(x) - F_d x p_{d-1,n} (x)), $$ and then monic polynomials with two close roots by $$ \eqalign{ r_{2d+1,n} (x) & = xs_{d,n}^2(x) + F_d^2 p_{d,n}^2 (x), \cr r_{2d,n}(x) & = s_{d,n}^2 (x) + F_{d-1}^2 x p_{d-1,n}^2 (x). \cr} \eqno (5) $$
nodes.statement_short: Builds $s_{d,n}$ from $p_{d,n},p_{d-1,n}$ with Fibonacci coefficients, then $r_{2d+1,n}$ and $r_{2d,n}$ as sums of squares (5).
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: Monicity of $s_{d,n}$ and $r_{d,n}$
nodes.statement: We claim that these polynomials are monic.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: Proof that $s_{d,n}$ is monic
nodes.statement: It suffices to show that this is true for $s_{d,n}(x)$. Since the leading coefficient of $p_{d,n} (x)$ is $F_d n + F_{d-2}$, we deduce that the leading coefficient of $s_{d,n}(x)$ is equal to \begin{eqnarray*} & (-1)^{d-1} (F_{d-1}(F_d n + F_{d-2})-F_d(F_{d-1}n + F_{d-3})) \\ & = (-1)^{d-1}(F_{d-1}F_{d-2}-F_dF_{d-3}) = 1. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $s_{d,n}$ and compute its leading coefficient, which collapses to $1$ by the Fibonacci identity $F_{d-1}F_{d-2}-F_dF_{d-3}=(-1)^{d-1}$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: Reduction to $s_{d,n}$
nodes.statement: It suffices to show that this is true for $s_{d,n}(x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Observe it is enough to prove monicity for $s_{d,n}$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: Computation of the leading coefficient
nodes.statement: Since the leading coefficient of $p_{d,n} (x)$ is $F_d n + F_{d-2}$, we deduce that the leading coefficient of $s_{d,n}(x)$ is equal to \begin{eqnarray*} & (-1)^{d-1} (F_{d-1}(F_d n + F_{d-2})-F_d(F_{d-1}n + F_{d-3})) \\ & = (-1)^{d-1}(F_{d-1}F_{d-2}-F_dF_{d-3}) = 1. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Expand the leading coefficient and simplify with a Fibonacci identity to obtain $1$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: Value of $r_{d,n}$ at $x_n$
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: Degree of $r_{d,n}(x)$
nodes.statement: Observe that the degree of the polynomial $r_{d,n} (x)$ is $d$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
conclusions: the degree of the polynomial $r_{d,n} (x)$ is $d$

nodes.name: Two complex conjugate roots of $r_{d,n}$ near $x_n$ (equation (6))
nodes.statement: We claim that $r_{d,n} (x)$ has two complex conjugate roots $v_{d,n}$ and $\overline{v_{d,n}}$ close to $x_n $, more precisely they are equal to $$ \eqalign{ 1/n-1/n^2+2/n^3- & 5/n^4+13/n^5- \ldots + \cr & + (-1)^d F_{2d-5}/n^{d-1} \pm i/n^{(2d-1)/2} + O(1/n^{d}). \cr} \eqno (6) $$
nodes.statement_short: $r_{d,n}$ has a conjugate pair $v_{d,n},\overline{v_{d,n}}$ within $n^{-(2d-1)/2}$ of $x_n$, with the expansion (6).
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
conclusions: r_{d,n} (x)$ has two complex conjugate roots $v_{d,n}$ and $\overline{v_{d,n}}$ close to $x_n

nodes.name: Proof of the location of the conjugate roots (6)
nodes.statement: Indeed, the polynomials $F_d^2 p_{d,n}^2(x)$ and $F_{d-1}^2 x p_{d-1,n}^2(x)$ have double roots $y_{d+1,n}$ and $y_{d,n}$, resp., in the disc $|x-x_n|\leq 1/n^{2d+1}$, resp. $|x-x_n|\leq 1/n^{2d-1}$. Moreover, we have $F_d^2 p_{d,n}^2(x) < xs_{d,n}^2(x)$ when $|x-x_n| = 1/n^{2d+1}$ and $F_{d-1}^2 x p_{d-1,n}^2(x) < s_{d,n}^2(x)$ when $|x-x_n| = 1/n^{2d-1}$. Hence, by Rouch\'e's theorem, the polynomial $r_{d,n} (x)$ has two roots $v$ satisfying $|v-x_n |<1/n^{d-1}$. Using a complex version of Taylor's theorem, by writing the roots $v$ of $r_{d,n} (x)$ close to $x_n$ as $v =x_n +\beta+\gamma i$ with $\gamma > 0$, we get $$ \eqalign{ 0 & =r_{d,n}(x_n +\beta+\gamma i) \cr & = r_{d,n}(x_n ) + (\beta+\gamma i)r'_{d,n}(x_n )+ (\beta+\gamma i)^2r''_{d,n}(x_n )/2+ O(1/n^{3d-5}). \cr} $$ Note that we have $$ r'_{2d+1,n}(x_n ) =\frac{2F_dF_{d+1}}{n^{2d-1}} + O(1/n^{2d}), $$ $$ r'_{2d,n}(x_n ) =\frac{2F_{d-1}F_{d-2}}{n^{2d-2}} + O(1/n^{2d-1}), $$ and $$ r''_{d,n}(x_n ) = 2F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^2 n^2 + O(n). $$ By considering imaginary parts in the above Taylor's formula we get \begin{eqnarray*} \beta &=& - \frac{r'_{d,n}(x_n)}{r''_{d,n}(x_n)} + O(\gamma^{-1}r''_{d,n}(x_n)^{-1}n^{-3d+5}) \\ &=& - \frac{F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor + (-1)^d}}{n^d} + O\left(\frac{1}{n^{d+1}}\right) + O\left(\frac{1}{\gamma n^{3d-3}}\right). \end{eqnarray*} Since the distance between the roots $x_n +\beta+\gamma i$ and $x_n +\beta-\gamma i$ of $r_{d,n} (x)$ is equal to $2 \gamma$ and $H(r_{d,n})=O(n^2)$, it follows from Mahler's theorem \cite{Mah64} quoted in the introduction that $\gamma \gg 1/n^{2d-2}$. Thus, $\beta = O(1/n^{d-1})$. Moreover, $\beta = O(1/n^d)$, unless $\gamma \ll 1/n^{2d-3}$. Looking at real parts leads to $$ \eqalign{ \frac{F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^2}{n^{2d-3}} + \frac{2\beta F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor + (-1)^d}}{n^{d-2}} + (\beta^2 - \gamma^2) & F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^2 n^2 \cr & = O\left(\frac{1}{n^{2d-2}}\right).} \eqno{(7)} $$ The assumption that $\gamma \ll 1/n^{2d-3}$ leads to a contradiction, by considering (7) as a quadratic equation in $\beta$. Hence, we have $\beta = O(1/n^{d})$. Now (7) gives $\gamma^2 = 1/n^{2d-1} + O(1/n^{2d})$, i.e., $\gamma = 1/n^{(2d-1)/2} + O(1/n^d)$, as claimed in (6).
nodes.statement_short: Rouché's theorem confines two roots near $x_n$; a complex Taylor expansion, Mahler's theorem and a contradiction on $\gamma$ pin down $\beta=O(n^{-d})$ and $\gamma=n^{-(2d-1)/2}+O(n^{-d})$.

nodes.name: Double roots of the two summands
nodes.statement: Indeed, the polynomials $F_d^2 p_{d,n}^2(x)$ and $F_{d-1}^2 x p_{d-1,n}^2(x)$ have double roots $y_{d+1,n}$ and $y_{d,n}$, resp., in the disc $|x-x_n|\leq 1/n^{2d+1}$, resp. $|x-x_n|\leq 1/n^{2d-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Locate the double roots of the squared summands in small discs around $x_n$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: Domination on the circles
nodes.statement: Moreover, we have $F_d^2 p_{d,n}^2(x) < xs_{d,n}^2(x)$ when $|x-x_n| = 1/n^{2d+1}$ and $F_{d-1}^2 x p_{d-1,n}^2(x) < s_{d,n}^2(x)$ when $|x-x_n| = 1/n^{2d-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Verify the strict inequalities needed on each circle.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: Apply Rouch\'e's theorem
nodes.statement: Hence, by Rouch\'e's theorem, the polynomial $r_{d,n} (x)$ has two roots $v$ satisfying $|v-x_n |<1/n^{d-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Rouché's theorem yields two roots of $r_{d,n}$ within $n^{-(d-1)}$ of $x_n$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: Complex Taylor expansion at $x_n$
nodes.statement: Using a complex version of Taylor's theorem, by writing the roots $v$ of $r_{d,n} (x)$ close to $x_n$ as $v =x_n +\beta+\gamma i$ with $\gamma > 0$, we get $$ \eqalign{ 0 & =r_{d,n}(x_n +\beta+\gamma i) \cr & = r_{d,n}(x_n ) + (\beta+\gamma i)r'_{d,n}(x_n )+ (\beta+\gamma i)^2r''_{d,n}(x_n )/2+ O(1/n^{3d-5}). \cr} $$
nodes.statement_short: Write $v=x_n+\beta+\gamma i$ and expand $r_{d,n}$ to second order.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: Derivative estimates at $x_n$
nodes.statement_short: Compute the first and second derivatives of $r_{d,n}$ at $x_n$ asymptotically.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: Imaginary parts give $\beta$
nodes.statement: By considering imaginary parts in the above Taylor's formula we get \begin{eqnarray*} \beta &=& - \frac{r'_{d,n}(x_n)}{r''_{d,n}(x_n)} + O(\gamma^{-1}r''_{d,n}(x_n)^{-1}n^{-3d+5}) \\ &=& - \frac{F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor + (-1)^d}}{n^d} + O\left(\frac{1}{n^{d+1}}\right) + O\left(\frac{1}{\gamma n^{3d-3}}\right). \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Taking imaginary parts expresses $\beta$ as $-r'_{d,n}(x_n)/r''_{d,n}(x_n)$ plus errors.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: Mahler's theorem bounds $\gamma$ from below
nodes.statement: Since the distance between the roots $x_n +\beta+\gamma i$ and $x_n +\beta-\gamma i$ of $r_{d,n} (x)$ is equal to $2 \gamma$ and $H(r_{d,n})=O(n^2)$, it follows from Mahler's theorem \cite{Mah64} quoted in the introduction that $\gamma \gg 1/n^{2d-2}$. Thus, $\beta = O(1/n^{d-1})$. Moreover, $\beta = O(1/n^d)$, unless $\gamma \ll 1/n^{2d-3}$.
nodes.statement_short: Mahler's theorem applied to $H(r_{d,n})=O(n^2)$ gives $\gamma\gg n^{-(2d-2)}$ and hence $\beta=O(n^{-(d-1)})$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: Real parts give relation (7)
nodes.statement: Looking at real parts leads to $$ \eqalign{ \frac{F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^2}{n^{2d-3}} + \frac{2\beta F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor + (-1)^d}}{n^{d-2}} + (\beta^2 - \gamma^2) & F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^2 n^2 \cr & = O\left(\frac{1}{n^{2d-2}}\right).} \eqno{(7)} $$
nodes.statement_short: Taking real parts yields the quadratic relation (7) between $\beta$ and $\gamma$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: Contradiction rules out $\gamma \ll 1/n^{2d-3}$
nodes.statement: The assumption that $\gamma \ll 1/n^{2d-3}$ leads to a contradiction, by considering (7) as a quadratic equation in $\beta$. Hence, we have $\beta = O(1/n^{d})$.
nodes.statement_short: Treating (7) as a quadratic in $\beta$ contradicts the small-$\gamma$ assumption, forcing $\beta=O(n^{-d})$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: Value of $\gamma$
nodes.statement: Now (7) gives $\gamma^2 = 1/n^{2d-1} + O(1/n^{2d})$, i.e., $\gamma = 1/n^{(2d-1)/2} + O(1/n^d)$, as claimed in (6).
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $\gamma=n^{-(2d-1)/2}+O(n^{-d})$, establishing (6).
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: Real-part relation (7)
nodes.statement: $$ \eqalign{ \frac{F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^2}{n^{2d-3}} + \frac{2\beta F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor + (-1)^d}}{n^{d-2}} + (\beta^2 - \gamma^2) & F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^2 n^2 \cr & = O\left(\frac{1}{n^{2d-2}}\right).} \eqno{(7)} $$
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: The irreducible factor $R_{d,n}(x)$ and its degree $\delta$
nodes.statement: Let $R_{d,n}(x)$ be the irreducible factor of $r_{d,n}(x)$ having roots $v_{d,n}$ and $\overline{v_{d,n}}$. Denote by $\delta$ its degree.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: Height bound (8) for $R_{d,n}$
nodes.statement: Note that, since $H(r_{d,n})=O(n^2)$, Gelfond's inequality implies that $$ H(R_{d,n})=O(n^2). \eqno (8) $$
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: The resultant $\Res_{d,n}$
nodes.statement: Denote by $\Res_{d,n}$ the resultant of the polynomials $R_{d,n} (x)$ and $L_n(x)$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.genus: the resultant of the polynomials $R_{d,n} (x)$ and $L_n(x)$

nodes.name: Lower bound (9) for the resultant
nodes.statement: Since $\Res_{d,n}$ is a rational integer and $x_n$ is not a root of $R_{d,n} (x)$, we have $$ |\Res_{d,n}| \ge 1. \eqno (9) $$
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
assumptions: Since $\Res_{d,n}$ is a rational integer and $x_n$ is not a root of $R_{d,n} (x)$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement: Furthermore, the definition of the resultant of two polynomials (see e.g. \cite[p. 223]{BuLiv}) implies that (recall that $R_{d,n}(x)$ is monic) $$ |\Res_{d,n}| \le (n^2 + 3n+1)^{\delta} \prod_{t : R_{d,n} (t) = 0} \, |t - x_n|. $$ Since the product of the absolute values of all the roots of $R_{d,n} (x)$ different from $v_{d,n}$ and $\overline{v_{d,n}}$ is bounded from above by $\sqrt{d+1}$ times the height of $R_{d,n} (x)$ (see \cite[Exercise A.1]{BuLiv}), we deduce from (6) and (8) that $$ |\Res_{d,n}| \ll n^{2 \delta} n^{-2d+1} n^2. $$ Combined with (9), this gives $2 \delta \ge 2d - 3$, thus $$ \delta \in \{d, d-1\}. $$ This implies that either $r_{d,n}(x)$ is irreducible, or it has an integer root (recall that any rational root of a monic polynomial must be a rational integer). Assume that $r_{d,n}(x)$ is reducible, i.e., that it has an integer root. This integer must divide $r_{d,n}(0)=F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^2$, and, by (5), it is of the form $-\alpha^2$ for an integer $\alpha$ dividing $F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}$. So, for any given degree $d$, there are only finitely many possibilities for the integer root of $r_{d,n}(x)$. Write $r_{d,n}(x)$ as $$ r_{d,n}(x)=A_d(x)n^2+B_d(x)n+C_d(x). $$ By the definition of $r_{d,n}(x)$ and (1), it follows easily by induction that the discriminant $B_d(x)^2 - 4A_d(x)C_d(x)$ of $r_{d,n}(x)$ with respect to $n$ is equal to $-4 F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^4 x^{2d-1}$. In particular, this discriminant is nonzero at $x=-\alpha^2$, and thus at least one of the numbers $A_d(-\alpha^2)$, $B_d(-\alpha^2)$, $C_d(-\alpha^2)$ is nonzero. This shows that $r_{d,n}(x)$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Z}[n,x]$. Furthermore, for given $\alpha$ there are exactly two (rational) values of $n$ such that $-\alpha^2$ is a root of $r_{d,n}(x)$. Hence, for sufficiently large positive integer $n$, the polynomial $r_{d,n}(x)$ has no integer roots, and therefore it is irreducible over $\mathbb{Z}[x]$. Since $$ {\rm sep}(r_{d,n}) = O(n^{-(d-1/2)}), $$ we obtain $$ e_{{\rm irr}}^* (d) \geq \frac{2d-1}{4}, $$ which proves Theorem \ref{tm3}.
nodes.statement_short: Resultant bounds force $\delta\in\{d,d-1\}$; a discriminant computation excludes integer roots of $r_{d,n}$, so $r_{d,n}$ is irreducible and its separation gives the bound.

nodes.name: Upper bound for the resultant
nodes.statement: Furthermore, the definition of the resultant of two polynomials (see e.g. \cite[p. 223]{BuLiv}) implies that (recall that $R_{d,n}(x)$ is monic) $$ |\Res_{d,n}| \le (n^2 + 3n+1)^{\delta} \prod_{t : R_{d,n} (t) = 0} \, |t - x_n|. $$

nodes.name: Estimate of the root product
nodes.statement: Since the product of the absolute values of all the roots of $R_{d,n} (x)$ different from $v_{d,n}$ and $\overline{v_{d,n}}$ is bounded from above by $\sqrt{d+1}$ times the height of $R_{d,n} (x)$ (see \cite[Exercise A.1]{BuLiv}), we deduce from (6) and (8) that $$ |\Res_{d,n}| \ll n^{2 \delta} n^{-2d+1} n^2. $$
nodes.statement_short: Use (6), (8) and a Mahler-type root-product bound to get $|\Res_{d,n}|\ll n^{2\delta-2d+3}$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: Dichotomy for the degree $\delta$
nodes.statement: Combined with (9), this gives $2 \delta \ge 2d - 3$, thus $$ \delta \in \{d, d-1\}. $$ This implies that either $r_{d,n}(x)$ is irreducible, or it has an integer root (recall that any rational root of a monic polynomial must be a rational integer).
nodes.statement_short: Comparing with (9) forces $\delta\in\{d,d-1\}$, so $r_{d,n}$ is irreducible or has an integer root.

nodes.name: Shape of a hypothetical integer root
nodes.statement: Assume that $r_{d,n}(x)$ is reducible, i.e., that it has an integer root. This integer must divide $r_{d,n}(0)=F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^2$, and, by (5), it is of the form $-\alpha^2$ for an integer $\alpha$ dividing $F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}$. nodes.name: Write $r_{d,n}$ as a quadratic in $n$
nodes.statement: Write $r_{d,n}(x)$ as $$ r_{d,n}(x)=A_d(x)n^2+B_d(x)n+C_d(x). $$
nodes.statement_short: Regard $r_{d,n}(x)$ as a quadratic polynomial in $n$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: Discriminant with respect to $n$
nodes.statement: By the definition of $r_{d,n}(x)$ and (1), it follows easily by induction that the discriminant $B_d(x)^2 - 4A_d(x)C_d(x)$ of $r_{d,n}(x)$ with respect to $n$ is equal to $-4 F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^4 x^{2d-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: By induction, the discriminant in $n$ equals $-4F_{\lfloor(d-1)/2\rfloor}^4x^{2d-1}$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: Irreducibility over $\mathbb{Z}[n,x]$
nodes.statement: In particular, this discriminant is nonzero at $x=-\alpha^2$, and thus at least one of the numbers $A_d(-\alpha^2)$, $B_d(-\alpha^2)$, $C_d(-\alpha^2)$ is nonzero. This shows that $r_{d,n}(x)$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Z}[n,x]$.
nodes.statement_short: Nonvanishing of the discriminant at $-\alpha^2$ shows $r_{d,n}$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Z}[n,x]$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: No integer roots for large $n$
nodes.statement: Furthermore, for given $\alpha$ there are exactly two (rational) values of $n$ such that $-\alpha^2$ is a root of $r_{d,n}(x)$. Hence, for sufficiently large positive integer $n$, the polynomial $r_{d,n}(x)$ has no integer roots, and therefore it is irreducible over $\mathbb{Z}[x]$.
nodes.statement_short: Only two rational $n$ per $\alpha$ admit the root $-\alpha^2$, so $r_{d,n}$ is irreducible for large $n$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: Conclusion of the separation bound
nodes.statement: Since $$ {\rm sep}(r_{d,n}) = O(n^{-(d-1/2)}), $$ we obtain $$ e_{{\rm irr}}^* (d) \geq \frac{2d-1}{4}, $$ which proves Theorem \ref{tm3}.
nodes.statement_short: From $\sep(r_{d,n})=O(n^{-(d-1/2)})$ and $H(r_{d,n})=O(n^2)$ conclude $e_{\rm irr}^*(d)\ge(2d-1)/4$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: Mahler's lower bound (10) for products of root differences
nodes.statement: Mahler's upper bound $e(d) \le d-1$ quoted in the Introduction is a particular case of the lower bound $$ \prod_{1\le i<j\le k} \vert \alpha_i -\alpha_j \vert \gg H(P)^{- d +1}, \eqno (10) $$ valid for any integer polynomial $P(x)$ of degree $d$ having at least $k \ge 2$ distinct roots $\alpha_1, \ldots , \alpha_k$, established in \cite{Mah64}.
nodes.statement_short: For any degree-$d$ integer polynomial with $k\ge2$ distinct roots, $\prod_{i<j}|\alpha_i-\alpha_j| \gg H(P)^{-d+1}$.
nodes.section: 5 Clusters of roots
assumptions: valid for any integer polynomial $P(x)$ of degree $d$ having at least $k \ge 2$ distinct roots $\alpha_1, \ldots , \alpha_k$

nodes.name: The cluster exponents $E(d,k)$, $E_{{\rm irr}}(d,k)$, $E^*(d,k)$, $E_{{\rm irr}}^*(d,k)$
nodes.statement: In \cite{BM2} the authors extended the definition of $e(d)$ to clusters of at least $3$ roots. Let $k$ and $d$ be integers with $2 \le k \le d$. We denote by $E(d,k)$, respectively $E_{{\rm irr}}(d,k)$, the infimum of the real numbers $\delta$ for which $$ \prod_{1\le i<j\le k} \vert \alpha_i -\alpha_j \vert \ge H(P)^{- \delta} $$ holds for every integer polynomial $P(x)$, respectively, irreducible integer polynomial $P(x)$, of degree $d$ and sufficiently large height, with distinct roots $\alpha_1, \ldots , \alpha_d$. We further use the notation $E^*(d,k)$, respectively $E_{{\rm irr}}^*(d,k)$, when we restrict our attention to monic integer polynomials, respectively monic integer irreducible polynomials.
nodes.statement_short: $E(d,k)$ and its variants are the infima of $\delta$ for which $\prod_{i<j\le k}|\alpha_i-\alpha_j| \ge H(P)^{-\delta}$ holds for large-height degree-$d$ polynomials.
nodes.section: 5 Clusters of roots
nodes.genus: the infimum of the real numbers $\delta$
differentia: holds for every integer polynomial $P(x)$, respectively, irreducible integer polynomial $P(x)$, of degree $d$ and sufficiently large height, with distinct roots $\alpha_1, \ldots , \alpha_d$

nodes.name: Upper bound $d-1$ for the cluster exponents
nodes.statement: We deduce from (10) that the quantities $E(d,k)$ and $E^* (d, k)$ are all bounded from above by $d-1$.
nodes.section: 5 Clusters of roots
conclusions: the quantities $E(d,k)$ and $E^* (d, k)$ are all bounded from above by $d-1$

nodes.name: Previously known cluster lower bounds (11)
nodes.statement: Regarding lower bounds, it is proved in \cite{BM1,BM2} that, for any integer $d \ge 4$ and any integer $k\ge 2$ that divides $d$, we have $$ E(d, k) \ge \frac{k-1}{k} d \quad \mbox{and} \quad E^* (d, k) \ge \frac{k-1}{k} d - \frac{k-1}{2}. \eqno (11) $$ In fact, the results from \cite{BM1,BM2} show that these bounds are valid also for $E_{{\rm irr}} (d, k)$ and $E_{{\rm irr}}^* (d, k)$, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: For $k \mid d$, $E(d,k)\ge \frac{k-1}{k}d$ and $E^*(d,k)\ge \frac{k-1}{k}d-\frac{k-1}{2}$, also valid in the irreducible cases.
nodes.section: 5 Clusters of roots
assumptions: for any integer $d \ge 4$ and any integer $k\ge 2$ that divides $d$
conclusions: E(d, k) \ge \frac{k-1}{k} d \quad \mbox{and} \quad E^* (d, k) \ge \frac{k-1}{k} d - \frac{k-1}{2}

nodes.name: The constructions strengthen (11)
nodes.statement: The constructions presented in the Sections 2 and 3 allow us to strengthen the estimates (11).
nodes.section: 5 Clusters of roots

nodes.name: Theorem 4 (cluster lower bounds (12) and (13))
nodes.statement: For every integer $k \ge 3$, there exist rational numbers $c_1(k)$ and $c_2(k)$ such that, for every integer $d \ge k$, we have $$ E(d,k) \geq \frac{k}{k+1} d - c_1 (k) \eqno (12) $$ and $$ E^* (d,k) \geq \frac{k}{k+1} d - c_2 (k). \eqno (13) $$ In particular, the exponent $-d+1$ in (10) cannot be replaced by $- \alpha_k d$, for a real number $\alpha_k$ less than $k/(k+1)$, even if the polynomial $P(x)$ in (10) is assumed to be monic.
nodes.statement_short: For each $k\ge3$ there are constants $c_1(k),c_2(k)$ with $E(d,k)\ge \frac{k}{k+1}d-c_1(k)$ and $E^*(d,k)\ge \frac{k}{k+1}d-c_2(k)$, so $\alpha_k<k/(k+1)$ is impossible in (10).
nodes.section: 5 Clusters of roots
conclusions: the exponent $-d+1$ in (10) cannot be replaced by $- \alpha_k d$, for a real number $\alpha_k$ less than $k/(k+1)$, even if the polynomial $P(x)$ in (10) is assumed to be monic

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4
nodes.statement: Let $\delta \ge 2$ and $h \ge 0$ be integers. The polynomial $$ {\tilde P}_{\delta, h, n} (x) := P_{\delta, n} (x) \times p_{\delta,n} (x) \times \cdots \times p_{\delta+h, n} (x) $$ has degree $(h+2)\delta + h(h+1)/2$, height $\ll n^{h+4}$, and it has a cluster of $h+3$ roots close to each other. Setting $k = h+3$, a short calculation gives (12), since one can multiply ${\tilde P}_{\delta, h, n} (x)$ by a suitable power of the monomial $x$. To get (13), it suffices, for $\delta$ even, to consider the polynomial $$ {\tilde Q}_{\delta, h, n} (x) := Q_{\delta, n} (x) \times q_{\delta,n} (x) \times \cdots \times q_{\delta + 2 h, n} (x), $$ multiplied by a suitable power of the monomial $x$. We omit the details.
nodes.statement_short: Multiply the families of Sections 2 and 3 together to build polynomials with a cluster of $h+3$ close roots, then compute.

nodes.name: Cluster construction for (12)
nodes.statement: Let $\delta \ge 2$ and $h \ge 0$ be integers. The polynomial $$ {\tilde P}_{\delta, h, n} (x) := P_{\delta, n} (x) \times p_{\delta,n} (x) \times \cdots \times p_{\delta+h, n} (x) $$ has degree $(h+2)\delta + h(h+1)/2$, height $\ll n^{h+4}$, and it has a cluster of $h+3$ roots close to each other. Setting $k = h+3$, a short calculation gives (12), since one can multiply ${\tilde P}_{\delta, h, n} (x)$ by a suitable power of the monomial $x$.
nodes.statement_short: Form $\tilde P_{\delta,h,n}$ as a product of $P_{\delta,n}$ and successive $p_{j,n}$, giving a cluster of $h+3$ roots and (12).
nodes.section: 5 Clusters of roots

nodes.name: Monic cluster construction for (13)
nodes.statement: To get (13), it suffices, for $\delta$ even, to consider the polynomial $$ {\tilde Q}_{\delta, h, n} (x) := Q_{\delta, n} (x) \times q_{\delta,n} (x) \times \cdots \times q_{\delta + 2 h, n} (x), $$ multiplied by a suitable power of the monomial $x$. We omit the details.
nodes.statement_short: The analogous monic product $\tilde Q_{\delta,h,n}$ yields (13); details omitted.
